outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20 and further strikes reported on Nov 21 and into Nov 22 and Nov 23. Ukrenergo said planned outage schedules would be in effect around the clock on Monday, Nov 23, and again on Tuesday, Nov 24, in parts of the country because of those attacks
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by LB.ua at 7:20 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (11:20 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), by UNIAN at 8:59 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (12:59 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), and by UNN at 5:13 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (9:13 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), said that on Tuesday, Nov 24, scheduled power-supply restrictions would be in effect around the clock in parts of Ukraine because of the aftermath of Russian attacks on the energy system: hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 groups, or queues, for all categories of consumers, and capacity-limitation schedules for industrial consumers. UNIAN, citing Ukrenergo, said those 0.5 to 3.5 queues amounted to about 2 to 14 hours without power, and UNN likewise said one group means four hours without electricity, so Tuesday outages may last from 2 to 14 hours. UNIAN also summarized Tuesday regional schedules, saying that in Sumy and the Sumy region the total duration without power would be from six to 14 hours; that in Lviv and the Lviv region some queues had no outages scheduled and the rest would be switched off once for two to four and a half hours; that in Poltava and the Poltava region customers would be switched off four times a day, except for two half-queues with three and five periods, with each outage lasting from half an hour to three and a half hours; and that Kyiv schedules would be applied individually and should be checked through local operators. LB.ua, in the same Nov 23 report, said that at present the most difficult situation with electricity supply remained in Dnipropetrovsk and Odesa regions. Kyiv Independent, in an article dated 9:19 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (1:19 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), citing the private energy company DTEK, said Russian attacks on four DTEK energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast over Nov 21 and Nov 22 had left about 353,000 households without electricity, that emergency power cuts were in effect in Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, with regular outage schedules suspended there, and that other parts of the region were subject to scheduled cuts ordered by Ukrenergo; DTEK, as quoted in that report, said emergency repair crews had worked through the night and were continuing restoration, prioritizing critical infrastructure, but that damage to main transmission networks meant technicians could not yet reconnect all consumers, and it did not give a timeline for restoring power to all affected households. NV, in an article dated 3:46 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (7:46 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), and Delo.ua, also citing DTEK, gave the same figure of about 353,000 households and said a significant part of Dnipro, the city of Samar, and adjacent districts had been left without power. Earlier Monday, Kyiv Post, in an article dated 2:18 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (7:18 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), citing Ukraine's Energy Ministry and First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, said Russia had carried out 100 attacks on Ukraine's energy, oil, and gas infrastructure over the past week, contributing to 224 recorded damage incidents, and that power outages had continued to affect seven regions on Monday, Nov 23: Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Sumy, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Poltava, with the situation remaining particularly difficult in Odesa and Dnipropetrovsk regions. The same Kyiv Post report, citing Nekrasov, said energy workers had restored power to critical infrastructure facilities while repairs and efforts to reconnect households and businesses continued; that grid restrictions had been introduced in Dnipropetrovsk region to prevent further outages caused by overloads; that emergency power cuts remained in place in Kharkiv region because of previous damage and reduced voltage in the high-voltage transmission network, with scheduled outages to resume once the situation stabilized; and that Russian forces had also struck a gas-infrastructure facility in Dnipropetrovsk region in the previous days, injuring three employees. Kyiv Post also said that across most of Ukraine, hourly electricity outage schedules were in place on Nov 23, while industrial consumers faced power restrictions, and, citing Ukraine's Air Force data reported by Ukrainian media, that on the night of Nov 23 Russia launched 153 attack drones against Ukraine, including 60 jet-powered Shahed drones, alongside Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoys. An earlier Sunday night Ukrenergo statement, as reported by Censor.NET at 10:24 p.m. EET Sunday, Nov 22 (2:24 p.m. CT), by UNIAN at 11:13 p.m. EET Sunday (3:13 p.m. CT), by Focus, and by 24tv, had said that on Monday, Nov 23, planned electricity outages would be in effect around the clock in parts of the country: hourly outage schedules of 1 to 3.5 groups, or queues, for all categories of consumers, and capacity-restriction schedules for industry. UNIAN, in that Sunday night report, said those 1 to 3.5 queues amounted to approximately 4 to 16 hours a day for household consumers. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (7:55 a.m. EET Tuesday, Nov 24).

outages.place: Odesa and parts of Odesa district
outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20. Later on Monday, Nov 23, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper said scheduled power-outage timetables were being reinstated in place of emergency blackouts after energy workers restored damaged infrastructure, and DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi said repairs had made a return to stabilization schedules possible, while warning that the energy system remained vulnerable to significant loads
outages.affected: Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by LB.ua at 8:03 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (12:03 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), said that in Odesa and Odesa District, scheduled power-outage timetables were being reinstated in place of emergency blackouts, that the return to planned schedules had become possible because of continuous work by energy workers restoring damaged infrastructure, and that residents were being urged to use electricity sparingly so as not to overload the power system and cause new emergency outages. DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, in a Nov 23 statement on its website, said that thanks to difficult repairs and the restoration of equipment, energy workers had been able to return to stabilization schedules, that the energy system remained vulnerable to significant loads, and that customers should not turn on all electrical appliances at once when power returned, in order to avoid overloading the networks and causing new accidents; the company pointed customers to its website and chatbots for the current schedules. An earlier Monday statement by Kiper, as reported by Censor.NET at 12:35 p.m. EET Monday, Nov 23 (4:35 a.m. CT), by UNN at 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday (2:11 a.m. CT), and by Slovo i Dilo at 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (4:38 a.m. CT), had said the electricity-supply situation in Odesa region remained difficult but that measures were being taken to stabilize it; that emergency outages without schedules were still being applied because the damaged equipment could not yet supply all consumers at once; that all critical infrastructure and some consumers had already been energized; that water was available in all districts, with possible pumping interruptions in some apartment buildings; that 9 of 11 large boiler houses were operating, with 2 more plus the CHP being brought online; that heat had already been supplied to 186,000 subscribers; and that about 79,000 consumers remained temporarily without heating. Ukrenergo, as reported Monday morning by UNN and Slovo i Dilo, had said the situation in Odesa Oblast had been partially stabilized and that electricity supply to critical infrastructure in Odesa had been restored after overnight repair work. No official remaining-electricity-customer count after the earlier Friday DTEK figures was found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (7:55 a.m. EET Tuesday, Nov 24).
outages.updated: Nov 23, 2026, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper via LB.ua 8:03 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (= 12:03 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), on scheduled power-outage timetables being reinstated in Odesa and Odesa District in place of emergency blackouts after restoration of damaged infrastructure, with residents urged to use electricity sparingly; DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi Nov 23 website statement on a return to stabilization schedules, the system remaining vulnerable to significant loads, and a request not to turn on all appliances at once; earlier Monday Kiper statement via Censor.NET 12:35 p.m. EET Monday (= 4:35 a.m. CT), UNN 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday (= 2:11 a.m. CT), and Slovo i Dilo 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (= 4:38 a.m. CT), on a still-difficult supply situation, emergency outages then still being applied, all critical infrastructure and some consumers already energized, water in all districts, 9 of 11 large boiler houses operating, heat already supplied to 186,000 subscribers, and about 79,000 consumers temporarily without heating; Ukrenergo Monday morning statement via UNN and Slovo i Dilo that the Odesa Oblast situation had been partially stabilized and that critical infrastructure in Odesa had been restored; rechecked 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (7:55 a.m. EET Tuesday, Nov 24), no official remaining-electricity-customer count after the earlier Friday DTEK figures found

outages.place: Dnipro, Samar, and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianske, and Pavlohrad districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks on four DTEK energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast over Nov 21 and Nov 22, according to DTEK, which said most of the facilities had been struck before, that equipment was damaged and fires broke out at several sites, and that damage to main transmission networks meant not all consumers could yet be reconnected. Emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, where regular hourly schedules were not being applied
outages.affected: DTEK, as reported by Kyiv Independent in an article dated 9:19 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (1:19 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), by NV at 3:46 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (7:46 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), and by Delo.ua, said Russian attacks on four of its energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast over two days, Nov 21 and Nov 22, had left about 353,000 households without electricity. Those reports, citing DTEK, said a significant part of Dnipro, the city of Samar, and adjacent districts had been left without power; that the facilities were hit in Dnipro and surrounding areas, damaging equipment and causing fires at several sites; that most of the facilities had been struck before; and that no energy workers were injured in the recent attacks. DTEK said emergency repair crews had worked through the night and were continuing restoration efforts, prioritizing electricity supplies to critical infrastructure, but that damage to main transmission networks meant technicians could not yet reconnect all consumers, and it did not give a timeline for restoring power to all affected households. Emergency power cuts were in effect in Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, with regular outage schedules suspended there; other parts of the region were subject to scheduled cuts ordered by Ukrenergo. An earlier Monday morning account from Ukrenergo, as reported by UNN at 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday, Nov 23 (2:11 a.m. CT) and by Slovo i Dilo at 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (4:38 a.m. CT), had said the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast situation remained significantly more difficult, with hourly outage schedules in effect and overnight restoration work after significant damage from Russian attacks. Dnipropetrovsk regional council head Mykola Lukashuk, via Vidomo at 10:59 a.m. Monday (2:59 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), had said emergency outages remained in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianske, and Pavlohrad districts, where DTEK hourly schedules were not being applied, with an hourly schedule in effect for Central Energy Company (CEK) customers and a separate schedule for part of Pavlohrad. No later official remaining-customer count after the DTEK figure of about 353,000 households was found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (7:55 a.m. EET Tuesday, Nov 24).
outages.updated: Nov 23, 2026, DTEK via Kyiv Independent dated 9:19 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (= 1:19 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), NV 3:46 p.m. Monday (= 7:46 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), and Delo.ua, on about 353,000 households without power after attacks on four DTEK facilities on Nov 21-22, a significant part of Dnipro, Samar, and adjacent districts left without power, emergency cuts in Dnipro and four districts, scheduled cuts elsewhere in the region, overnight repairs prioritizing critical infrastructure, and no timeline for full restoration; earlier Monday morning Ukrenergo update via UNN 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday (= 2:11 a.m. CT) and Slovo i Dilo 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (= 4:38 a.m. CT), saying the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast situation remained significantly more difficult; Dnipropetrovsk regional council head Mykola Lukashuk via Vidomo 10:59 a.m. Monday (= 2:59 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), on emergency outages in Dnipro and four districts; rechecked 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (7:55 a.m. EET Tuesday, Nov 24), no later official remaining-customer count after the DTEK figure of about 353,000 households found

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said gas production at the Khor Mor field was expected to resume in the coming days after a Monday meeting of delegations from Erbil and Baghdad with the field's operator, Dana Gas; that, according to information acquired by The New Region, the outcome of the meeting was positive, with Dana Gas set to resume gas production in the next two to three days; and that a source at the field told The New Region that all employees at Khor Mor had returned to work, that Dana Gas was set to release a statement on the resumption of operations in the near future, that efforts to repair the damaged sections were also expected to begin soon, and that production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack. Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, told The New Region on Monday that electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, with supply gradually increasing, but that it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations for electricity production to return to pre-attack levels. Those reports did not say that Khor Mor production or pre-attack electricity supply had already resumed. An earlier Nov 22, 2026 report by The New Region had said the Monday meeting was planned to discuss resuming production, that Dana Gas was expected to insist on security guarantees against further attacks, and that if an agreement were reached on Monday, a specialized Turkish company would begin repairs estimated to take six days. Kurdistan24, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said the Nov 8 drone attack in Sulaimani province caused a large fire and stopped gas production entirely, with no casualties, and that the stoppage cut 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts of electricity in the Kurdistan Region and reduced power-supply hours by five to six hours a day. That account is consistent with earlier official figures: Al Jazeera, on Nov 9, citing Iraqi and Kurdish officials and the official Iraqi News Agency, said the attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power and, citing Omed Ahmed, that it suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal, and Duhok and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts off the grid. Rudaw later quoted Ahmed as saying authorities had increased generation from approximately 1,000 megawatts immediately after the attack to 1,550 megawatts, of which 50 megawatts were reserved for essential facilities and factories, leaving 1,500 megawatts for residents and raising daily public electricity supply to six to eight hours; Ahmed said the electricity then available covered only 40 percent of demand, leaving a 60 percent shortfall, and that no date had been established for production to resume. Rudaw's article image assets for that report are dated Nov 13, 2026. 964media, in a Nov 15 report, quoted Ahmed as saying that no timeframe had been set for supplies to return to normal and that within 48 hours of the attack generation had been increased from 1,000 megawatts to nearly 1,650 megawatts. Dana Gas, in a Nov 14 clarification later restated in coverage including a Kurdistan24 report, said the facility had sustained significant damage and that no gas could currently be produced. The Insight International, in a Nov 21 report citing private-generator officials who spoke to Rudaw on Saturday, Nov 21, said the public grid remained weak because of the gas shortfall and that neighborhood generators were still running for most of the day in Erbil, Sulaimani, and Duhok. No official customer count was given. No official confirmation that Khor Mor production had already resumed, and no later official ministry generation figure, was found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (8:55 a.m. Iraq time Tuesday, Nov 24).
outages.etr: No official firm restoration time was given. The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said Dana Gas was set to resume gas production in the next two to three days after a positive Monday meeting, that a source at the field said production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack, and that Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, said electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, though it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations to return to pre-attack electricity-production levels. As of those reports, Khor Mor production had not been confirmed as having already resumed. No later official confirmation that production had already resumed was found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (8:55 a.m. Iraq time Tuesday, Nov 24).

outages.place: Donetsk, Makiivka, Yenakiieve, Khartsyzk, Zuhres, Torez, Snizhne, and nearby districts
outages.cause: Attacks on energy infrastructure, including a massive attack on the night of Nov 22, 2026, according to occupation officials, who said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night and that new outages were added to the effects of earlier damage; occupation officials also described a power deficit and forced temporary outages to prevent accidents
outages.affected: The occupation utility Donetskenergo, a branch of JSC South-West Electric Grid Company, as reported Tuesday morning, Nov 24, by the local channels CHP Donetsk and Typical Donetsk and republished by TVGram at 7:55 a.m. Moscow time Tuesday (10:55 p.m. CT Monday) and also carried by Pressa24, said that 300 transformer substations remained partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk and that 48,460 subscribers remained without electricity, and that specialists were continuing restoration work and reconnection of customers. That Tuesday morning city figure indicated that the Monday evening expectation by occupation government head Andrei Chertkov, as reported by DAN at 6:34 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (9:34 a.m. CT if Moscow time), that electricity would be returned to all remaining consumers by the end of Monday, had not been confirmed as completed. The occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, as reported by DNR News at 3:19 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (6:19 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said that because of repair and restoration work after UAV strikes on the energy system, partial outages would be required on Tuesday, Nov 24, from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., affecting the Kuibyshev, Kievskyi, and Leninskyi districts of Donetsk; Mariupol and adjacent districts; Novoazovsky municipal district; and Volnovakha municipal district, and that the outages would be partial, with those territories not fully de-energized. Occupation government head Andrei Chertkov, as reported earlier by DAN at 6:34 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (9:34 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said that electricity had been restored to the majority of subscribers in the territory who had been without power over the previous two days after attacks, that a significant part of subscribers had already been reconnected, that work was continuing, and that they expected to return electricity to all remaining consumers by the end of Monday. Chertkov, as quoted by DAN, also said energy workers were having to repair new damage and return to sections where power had only recently been restored, and that a capacity deficit caused by damaged equipment was leading to temporary outages in some municipalities to avoid overloads and further accidents. That evening statement did not give a new remaining-customer count, and no official confirmation that all remaining customers had been restored by the end of Monday was found. The last official count found was from the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, as reported by RIA Novosti at 12:50 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (3:50 a.m. CT if Moscow time) and by DNR News at 9:48 a.m. Monday (12:48 a.m. CT if Moscow time), which said that as of Monday morning slightly more than 207,000 subscribers remained without electricity after attacks on the energy system. RIA Novosti, citing the ministry, said attacks on energy facilities had been repeated the previous night, that no specialists had been injured, and that partial outages had been recorded in Donetsk, Makiivka, the Amvrosiivka, Volnovakha, Telmanove, Shakhtarsk, and Yasynuvata municipal districts, and in Khartsyzk, Zuhres, Torez, Snizhne, and Yenakiieve. A morning report by Lenta novostei Donetska dated 9:32 a.m. Monday, Nov 23 (12:32 a.m. CT if Moscow time), also said 249 boiler houses had been stopped. The Makiivka occupation administration, as reported by Lenta novostei Makeevki at 7:16 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (10:16 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing the Makiivka city electric networks branch of the South-West Electric Grid Company, said that as of 6:20 p.m. Monday (9:20 a.m. CT if Moscow time) several districts remained without power because of emergency disconnections and increased load on the networks, including parts of the Chervonohvardeiske, Horniatske, Kirovskyi, and Tsentralno-Miskyi districts and part of the city center, and that heating might also be temporarily interrupted; that report did not give a customer count. Vedomosti, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, citing Donetsk occupation mayor Alexei Kulemzin and data from the Donetskenergo branch of the South-West Electric Grid Company, said 114,648 subscribers remained without electricity in Donetsk city, that partial outages had affected all districts of the city, and that 551 transformer substations were de-energized. An earlier Sunday statement by Chertkov, as reported by DNR News on Nov 22, had said more than 279,000 subscribers were without power after attacks. The Monday morning occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy figure of slightly more than 207,000 subscribers still out, covering a wider set of localities than the Tuesday morning Donetsk-city figure, was the last official ministry-wide count found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (8:55 a.m. Moscow time Tuesday, Nov 24).

outages.etr: Occupation government head Andrei Chertkov, as reported by DAN at 6:34 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (9:34 a.m. CT if Moscow time), said they expected to return electricity to all remaining consumers by the end of Monday; that expectation was not confirmed as completed. The occupation utility Donetskenergo, as reported Tuesday morning, Nov 24, by the local channels CHP Donetsk and Typical Donetsk and republished by TVGram at 7:55 a.m. Moscow time Tuesday (10:55 p.m. CT Monday), said 48,460 subscribers remained without electricity in Donetsk city. The occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, as reported by DNR News at 3:19 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (6:19 a.m. CT if Moscow time) and by Komsomolskaya Pravda at 12:33 p.m. Monday, Nov 23, said partial outages would be required on Tuesday, Nov 24, from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. in several districts of Donetsk, in Mariupol and adjacent districts, and in the Novoazovsky and Volnovakha municipal districts, for repair and restoration work. An earlier Sunday statement by Chertkov, as reported by DNR News at 5:45 p.m. Sunday, Nov 22 (8:45 a.m. CT if Moscow time), had said restoration of the damaged energy center would take roughly two to three weeks.

outages.place: Crimea, including Dzhankoy, Bilohirsk, Rozdolne, Bakhchysarai, Sovietskyi, Kirovskyi, and Pervomaiskyi districts, and parts of Feodosia, Yevpatoria, and Simferopol
outages.cause: A power-capacity shortage after strikes on transmission networks outside the peninsula, according to occupation sources. On Tuesday, Nov 24, Krymenergo said a consumption-restriction regime remained in effect by command of the federal system operator, with outages of about three to six hours. The acting head of the Lenine district occupation administration had also said daily rolling outages would be organized in that district from Nov 24 through Dec 3
outages.affected: Krymenergo, as reported by RIA Novosti Crimea at 8:37 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24, updated at 8:43 a.m. Tuesday (11:37 p.m. and 11:43 p.m. CT Monday if Moscow time), and by Krymskaya Gazeta at 8:11 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (11:11 p.m. CT Monday if Moscow time), said that on Tuesday, Nov 24, a consumption-restriction regime remained in effect in Crimea by command of the federal system operator, that electricity supply would be temporarily stopped for consumers on the peninsula, and that the approximate duration of the outages would be three to six hours, with additional notice if the outages were extended. outages.cause: Generation-capacity deficit in the national electric system. UNE's Monday bulletin said unit 1 of CTE Santa Cruz and unit 2 of CTE Felton were in breakdown, and that unit 3 of CTE Santa Cruz, unit 5 of CTE Nuevitas, unit 1 of CTE Felton, and unit 5 of CTE Renté were in maintenance, with thermal-generation limitations of 446 MW
outages.affected: The official UNE Monday bulletin, as published by Juventud Rebelde at 8:35 a.m. Cuba time Monday, Nov 23 (7:35 a.m. CT) and updated at 10:15 a.m. Cuba time Monday (9:15 a.m. CT), and as also published by Cubadebate on Nov 23, said Sunday's service was affected by a generation-capacity deficit throughout all 24 hours and that the affectation continued through the early-morning hours. The bulletin said that as of 6:00 a.m. Monday, Cuba time, 1,105 MW were available, demand was 2,135 MW, and 1,039 MW were affected; that a midday affectation of 1,200 MW was estimated; and that, if the forecast conditions held, a Monday evening-peak affectation of 1,725 MW was forecast against 1,105 MW available and 2,800 MW of maximum demand, a deficit of 1,695 MW. The published Monday bulletin text did not state the megawatt figure for Sunday's 6:50 p.m. peak. CiberCuba, in a report dated 11:35 a.m. Monday (10:35 a.m. CT if Cuba time), said Renté unit 3 had gone offline in an emergency at 9:01 a.m. Monday. An earlier official UNE Sunday bulletin, via Granma at 10:11 a.m. Cuba time Sunday (9:11 a.m. CT), had given Saturday's maximum affectation as 1,778 MW at 6:50 p.m. Cuba time Saturday and a Sunday peak forecast of 1,713 MW. CiberCuba's SEN observatory, updated Nov 23, said the national grid remained interconnected and that no total SEN collapse was recorded on Monday. No official Sunday evening-peak actual in megawatts, no official Monday evening-peak actual, and no official Tuesday UNE bulletin were found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (12:55 a.m. Cuba time Tuesday, Nov 24).

outages.cause: Planned electricity restrictions that Tavanir said began Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation
outages.affected: The National, in an article dated November 23, 2026, and marked updated at 5:00 a.m., said scheduled cuts had begun and quoted Tavanir CEO Mohammad Allahdad as saying the restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day if temperatures fall, and quoted President Masoud Pezeshkian, via Isna, on expected winter difficulties. Euronews Persian, in a report dated 7:42 a.m. GMT+1 Monday, Nov 23 (12:42 a.m. CT Monday), said planned electricity outages began on Sunday, Nov 22 (1 Azar 1405), that Tavanir had announced the cuts on Saturday because of fuel-supply limitations at power plants, and that electricity-industry officials in Khorasan Razavi, Qazvin, and Kermanshah had confirmed the start of the restrictions. The same Euronews report, citing Mashhad distribution-company spokesman Majid Hassan-Nejad, said each outage turn in Mashhad would last two hours, though it was not yet clear whether the restrictions would be applied daily or with a gap of several days; citing Qazvin distribution-company official Seyed Mohammad Ghaflabashi, that household and commercial customers there were subject to the restrictions; and, citing Mehr news agency and Kermanshah distribution-company CEO Seyed Hamed Hosseini, that two-hour outages in Kermanshah were being applied between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. Iran International, in a report dated 1:17 p.m. GMT Sunday, Nov 22 (7:17 a.m. CT), said scheduled cuts were resuming and that Sunday reports from Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz, Mashhad, Yazd, Kermanshah, and Ardabil described hours-long outages, often without notice, and quoted Allahdad on restrictions beginning Nov 22 because of fuel shortages. Nour News, in a report dated 8:09 a.m. Iran time Sunday, Nov 22, or 1 Azar 1405 (10:39 p.m. CT Saturday), and Eghtesad Online, in a report dated 8:29 a.m. Iran time Sunday (10:59 p.m. CT Saturday) that cited Nour News, said planned electricity restrictions began that day and, citing the Tavanir chief executive, that the new restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day, that the timing is not fixed and may change with network conditions, and that customers would be informed through the Bargh-e Man system and app, the Bale messenger app, and text messages. Tavanir had announced on Saturday, Nov 21, that planned electricity restrictions on households and businesses would begin on Sunday, Nov 22, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation, according to Iran International in a report dated 5:11 p.m. GMT Saturday, Nov 21 (11:11 a.m. CT), and to RFE/RL. Anar News, in a report updated at 12:05 a.m. UTC Sunday, Nov 22 (6:05 p.m. CT Saturday), citing BBC Persian, also said planned power outages began in Iran on Sunday, Nov 22, because of fuel shortages at power plants. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (9:25 a.m. Iran time Tuesday, Nov 24).

outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike; he said affected areas continued to experience prolonged outages and scheduled power cuts as of this week. The report said the Sudan Electricity Holding Company and Ministry of Energy had yet to publicly announce the restoration of the major facilities damaged in the attacks. A United Nations report published Nov 17, issued in Geneva and posted on the UN in Sudan website, said that in just over two weeks between Oct 20 and Nov 4, 29 drone strikes, attributed to the Rapid Support Forces, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations across 11 states, triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines. An earlier Al Jazeera Nov 15 feature said there is no clear schedule for the resulting power cuts, which can last anywhere between six hours and a day, and, citing The Associated Press, said repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100 MW. Residents and a small-business owner in Port Sudan described prolonged, unreliable cuts, including outages lasting more than 24 hours. Al-Ghad Al-Sudani, in a report last updated Nov 22, 2026, said explosions and drone flights returned to Khartoum on Sunday morning, Nov 22, amid reports of attacks on military sites in various parts of the capital, and that the attacks coincided with power outages in large parts of the city; the report did not give a customer count or independently establish the cause of that outage. No later official national customer count or restoration timetable was found as of 11:55 PM CT Monday, Nov 23 (7:55 a.m. Sudan time Tuesday, Nov 24).
